subsection: 7. The impact of EEC membership; case study: the impact of the EEC on fisheries

notes.h: Background: why Ireland joined a common market
notes.b: By 1973 Ireland had already spent fifteen years moving away from protection, and it still depended heavily on the British market. Those two facts explain both why entry was sought and why its effects were mixed.
points: Before 1958 Ireland was protectionist (it shielded home industry with tariffs, taxes on imports) and its economy was stagnant. The First Programme for Economic Expansion, 1958 to 1963, and Seán Lemass's policies began to move it towards free trade.

The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement of 1965 cut tariffs on trade with Britain, so protected Irish industries already faced competition before 1973. This is why entry deepened an existing trend rather than starting it.
Ireland depended heavily on the British market for exports, above all farm produce.
Ireland's application of 1961 fell when de Gaulle vetoed British entry in 1963, and he vetoed it again in 1967. Ireland and Britain were finally admitted together.
The 1972 referendum approved entry, with about 83 per cent voting yes, under a Fianna Fáil government led by Jack Lynch. There is more on this in the notes on the UN and the EEC.
The economic problems of the 1970s and 1980s (oil price shocks, inflation, unemployment, debt and emigration) are the setting in which the gains and costs of membership have to be judged.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to name the date of entry and at least two dated measures, so learn the dates here as a frame for the whole topic.

notes.h: Key concept: the common market and the terms to know
notes.b: The European Economic Community (EEC) was built as a common market, meaning its members traded with one another as if they were a single economy. Several technical terms recur through this topic, so each is defined here as it is used.
points: A common market means free trade among its members, a common external tariff (one shared tax on goods from outside), and free movement of goods, workers and capital across member borders.

The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) was the EEC's system of farm support. Intervention meant the EEC buying surplus produce into storage at a guaranteed price, so that market prices could not fall below a floor.
A quota is a limit on how much a farmer or fishing state may produce or land. A derogation is a temporary exemption from a general rule, such as the one Ireland won on fishing limits.

A total allowable catch (TAC) is the whole limit set for a fish species. Relative stability is the rule that divides a TAC into national quotas according to each state's past catches. Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM) is the Irish state fisheries board.
The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) gave money to poorer regions. A directive is an EEC instruction that member states must turn into their own national law.
notes.tip: Short-answer questions ask what the CAP was and what the ERDF did, so be ready to define each in one clear sentence.

notes.b: On 1 January 1973 Ireland joined the EEC, together with Britain and Denmark, which raised the Community from six members to nine. Membership changed how Ireland traded, who made its laws and where its money came from.
points: Tariffs on industrial trade with other members were phased out over a transition period ending in 1977, and farm prices were brought into line in stages over about five years. Ireland also adopted the common external tariff on goods from outside the Community.

EEC law took precedence over Irish law in the areas covered by the treaties. The Third Amendment to the Constitution, approved by referendum in May 1972, made this possible by allowing the state to join and giving EEC law effect in Ireland.

Irish ministers sat on the Council of Ministers, Irish members sat in the European Parliament, and Patrick Hillery was the first Irish member of the Commission, serving from 1973 to 1976. The other main institution was the European Court of Justice.
Ireland held the presidency of the Council of Ministers for the first time from January to June 1975, which gave a small state a turn at chairing the Community's business.
Membership reduced dependence on Britain. Britain took well over half of Irish exports in the early 1970s and only about a third by the late 1980s, because trade with the continent grew.

Net payments from the EEC budget to Ireland (what it received minus what it paid in) amounted to several per cent of national income by the 1980s. This helped to pay for farm support, training and infrastructure.
Ireland joined the European Monetary System in March 1979, a scheme to keep member currencies stable against one another. Britain stayed out, so the Irish pound broke its link with sterling.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the May 1972 referendum, the 1972 accession treaty and entry on 1 January 1973. Give the right date for each.

notes.h: Agriculture and the Common Agricultural Policy
notes.b: Farming was the sector with most to gain from entry, because the CAP promised farmers prices that Irish producers had never been guaranteed. The gains were large, but they were not shared equally and they brought a new problem of surplus.
points: The CAP guaranteed minimum prices for products such as beef, milk and cereals, and bought surplus produce into intervention stores. Farmers therefore knew they could sell at a fixed floor price.
Irish farm prices were raised towards EEC levels during the transition. Farm incomes rose sharply in the early years of membership, especially for beef and dairy farmers.
Land values rose, and farmers invested in machinery, buildings and drainage, helped by grants, because higher guaranteed prices made the investment worth making.

The benefits were uneven. Larger and more productive farms in the east and south gained most, while small farms on poor land in the west gained less, because they had less produce to sell at the higher prices.
Guaranteed prices encouraged overproduction, because farmers produced more whatever the demand. In 1984 the EEC introduced milk quotas, limiting output on Irish dairy farms.
The number of people working on the land continued to fall, and agriculture's share of employment and output declined, even though farm incomes had risen.
notes.tip: Strong answers separate winners from losers. Say that large farmers in the east and south gained most and small western farmers least. Do not confuse milk quotas (1984) with fish quotas (1983).

notes.b: Alongside farm support, the EEC redistributed money to poorer places and people. Ireland was one of the poorer members, so it received a large share compared with its size.
points: The European Regional Development Fund was created in 1975, and Ireland, as one of the poorer members, was a leading beneficiary relative to its size.
The European Social Fund paid for training and employment schemes for young and unemployed people. It helped to pay for the training schemes of AnCO, the state training authority.
The funds were spent on roads, water and sewerage schemes, telecommunications and industrial estates, mainly under the direction of the Irish government.

A reform of the structural funds (the regional and social funds together) in 1988, linked to the Single European Act of 1987, roughly doubled the money available. Ireland's programme ran from 1989 to 1993.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the three: the ERDF (1975) is for regions, the Social Fund is for training, and the 1988 reform is the doubling of the structural funds.

notes.h: Foreign investment, industry and the decline of protected firms
notes.b: Membership opened the EEC market to anyone who produced inside Ireland, but it also stripped away the tariffs that had sheltered older Irish firms. New industry grew while old industry shrank.
points: American and other foreign firms set up factories in Ireland to sell into the EEC, drawn by Industrial Development Authority (IDA) grants, a young English-speaking workforce, low taxes and access to the EEC market.
From 1981 manufacturing profits were taxed at 10 per cent, which made Ireland even more attractive to firms looking for a low-tax base.

Electronics, pharmaceuticals, chemicals and engineering became leading sectors. Digital, for example, opened a plant in Galway in 1971, before entry, which shows the kind of foreign investment the IDA attracted.
Protected Irish industries such as clothing, textiles and footwear lost their tariff protection, and many firms closed with heavy job losses, because they could not compete with cheaper imports.

Employment in traditional manufacturing fell. The rise in unemployment of the late 1970s and 1980s showed that membership did not by itself solve the economy's weaknesses. There is more on this in the notes on the economic and social challenges of the 1970s and 1980s.
Irish exports became more diversified, and manufactured goods became the larger share of exports, overtaking farm produce in value.
notes.tip: Do not present Digital in Galway as a firm drawn by EEC membership. Date it 1971, before entry. In an essay, pair the new industries with the closures and unemployment.

notes.b: Membership changed Irish law and outlook as well as incomes. Some changes were required by EEC directives, while others coincided with entry.
points: The equal pay directive of 1975 and the equal treatment (employment) directive of 1976 required changes in Irish law. They reinforced the Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 and the Employment Equality Act 1977. There is more on this in the notes on the status of women.

The marriage bar (the rule forcing women to resign from the civil service on marrying) was lifted in 1973, the year of entry. It followed the Commission on the Status of Women rather than an EEC directive.
A directive on equal treatment in social welfare, adopted in 1978, forced Ireland to change payments to married women in the 1980s.
Irish citizens gained the right to live and work in other member states, which eased emigration, and young people had more contact with continental Europe, so attitudes became more outward-looking.
Irish judges were obliged to apply EEC law, and the European Court of Justice became a route for individuals to challenge Irish law.
Critics argued that membership cost Ireland some of its independence. The debate over sovereignty returned in the Crotty case and in the later referendums on European treaties.
notes.tip: Link the 1975 and 1976 directives to the 1974 and 1977 Irish Acts, but only if you have each date right. Also say that membership changed outlook and law, not only income, and that opponents warned of lost independence.

notes.h: Case study: the Irish fishing industry before 1973
notes.b: Irish fishing was small and under-developed, but it was important to coastal communities and became a sensitive issue in the accession negotiations. Knowing its state before entry explains why the terms mattered and why they were disputed.
points: Irish waters were rich in fish, but the industry was small. Most boats were old, small and inshore, and the fleet lacked the range to fish far from land.
Fishing employed only a few thousand full-time fishermen, concentrated in coastal counties, and many combined it with farming.
Irish consumers ate little fish outside Fridays, so the home market was small and the industry exported little.
Foreign trawlers fished close to the Irish coast under historic rights (long-established claims to fish there), because the exclusive Irish limit was narrow.
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), the state fisheries board, was created in 1952 to develop the industry through grants and loans for boats, training and marketing.
In the 1960s and early 1970s BIM helped to build a more modern fleet, including larger boats able to catch herring, whitefish and shellfish.
Fish made up a tiny share of Irish exports and national output before 1973, which is why governments treated the fishing terms as less important than the farming terms.
notes.tip: For a short answer on fishing, give the state of the industry before 1973: small, old inshore boats and foreign trawlers fishing under historic rights. BIM dates from 1952, before the EEC.

notes.h: Case study: the accession terms and the Common Fisheries Policy
notes.b: Fishing rules went through three stages: an equal-access principle in 1970, a temporary Irish exemption in 1973 and the Common Fisheries Policy of 1983, which was to be reviewed after ten years. Keeping the dates and terms straight is the key to this case study.
points: In 1970 the EEC agreed the principle of equal access for all members' fleets to Community waters, just as the applicant states opened negotiations.

Irish negotiators argued that fishing mattered to poor coastal communities. Ireland obtained a derogation: an exclusive six-mile zone for Irish boats, and a 12-mile zone in parts of the coast, for ten years to the end of 1982.

Other members could fish beyond those limits, and Irish boats gained access to British and Danish waters. Critics said the government gave away too much in order to secure the farming terms, and that fishing was treated as expendable.

In 1976, at The Hague, member states agreed to extend fishing limits to 200 nautical miles from 1 January 1977 and gave Ireland (and Britain) preferential treatment, known as the Hague preferences. This is not the 1969 Hague summit of EEC leaders.
Negotiating a new common policy took until January 1983, when member states agreed on the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), which replaced the temporary derogation that ended at the close of 1982.

The CFP set annual total allowable catches (TACs) for the main species, shared out as national quotas on the principle of relative stability, meaning shares based on past catches, with some preference for Ireland.
It reserved a 12-mile coastal belt for local fishermen, and the arrangements were to be reviewed after ten years.
Irish fishermen and ministers complained that Ireland's quotas were small compared with the value of the fish in its waters.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level answers must name the derogation's terms and years: six miles and 12 miles, to the end of 1982. Do not confuse the 1973 six-mile zone with the 1983 12-mile belt, or a TAC (the whole limit) with a quota (one state's share).

notes.h: Case study: development, ports and foreign fleets
notes.b: Grants turned a small inshore industry into a more modern one centred on a few ports, while foreign fleets and quota disputes kept the industry in the news.
points: With EEC and state grants, BIM financed new and larger vessels, and the Irish fleet grew in the late 1970s and 1980s.

Killybegs, Co. Donegal, developed into Ireland's leading fishing port, with a fleet of larger trawlers and pelagic boats (which catch fish such as herring that swim near the surface), processing factories and a growing service industry.
Castletownbere, Co. Cork, became a major whitefish port, with boats landing fish for sale and export.
Other ports, namely Dunmore East (Co. Waterford), Howth (Co. Dublin), Rossaveal (Co. Galway) and Kilmore Quay (Co. Wexford), also received investment in piers and harbours.
Foreign fleets fished in Irish waters, and the Irish Naval Service did fishery protection, inspecting and arresting vessels that broke the rules.
Spain and Portugal joined the EEC on 1 January 1986, after which Spanish vessels had a legal but limited route to Irish waters. Before then Spain was not a member.
Disputes over illegal fishing, over the size of quotas and over the shares given to other states recurred through the 1980s.
notes.tip: For the Ordinary Level fishing answer, name BIM with at least two ports and say what each is known for: Killybegs for its pelagic fleet and processing, Castletownbere for whitefish.

notes.h: Case study: benefits, costs and conflicting views
notes.b: Judging the EEC's impact on fishing means weighing real investment against real grievances. The two sides in the argument were the fishermen and the government, each with a case.
points: Benefits: investment in harbours, boats and processing plants created jobs in some coastal towns, and the 200-mile limit gave Ireland a large area of sea to manage.
Fish processing and exports to continental markets expanded through the 1980s, which widened the market for an industry that had once sold little abroad.
Costs: quotas limited what Irish boats could land, small inshore fishermen often lost out to larger vessels and fewer ports, and young people left declining harbours.
Fishermen's organisations claimed that Ireland received a small share of the fish caught in its own waters, and argued that the government treated fisheries as secondary to farming.
The government's side was that it had obtained the best terms it could, the 12-mile zone and the Hague preferences, and that fishing mattered little beside farming.
Supporters of EEC membership pointed to the new money for the industry. Opponents of entry, such as the Common Market Defence Campaign (1972), warned mainly of lost sovereignty in general.
The fishing industry remained a source of grievance, and its history became a standard example in debates on the costs of membership.
notes.tip: Give a mixed verdict: new investment and a large sea area against small quotas, foreign fleets and grievance. Do not credit the Common Market Defence Campaign with the fishing complaint, which came from fishermen's organisations and critics of the terms.

notes.h: Assessment: the gains and losses of membership
notes.b: Examiners reward a clear judgement backed by paired points, so weigh what membership achieved against what it failed to do, and say who gained and who lost.
points: Achievements: secure and better-priced markets for farmers, large transfers from Europe, foreign investment in new industries, equality legislation and a wider international outlook.
Limits: protected firms closed, unemployment rose in the 1980s, small farms and the west benefited least, and the fishing industry gained less than farming.
Contemporary view: supporters said membership was the only way to modernise an economy that relied on protection and emigration; opponents said it threatened sovereignty and traditional industries.

Later view: historians generally accept that membership underpinned the transformation of the economy and society, while stressing that the full benefits came later, from the 1990s, and that farmers and fishermen did not all gain equally.
notes.tip: Open your essay with a judgement, then give dated pairs of points. Divide winners (large farmers, exporters) from losers (small western farmers, textile workers, fishermen) and separate the 1970s effects from the longer view of the 1990s.

keyTerms.definition: A group of countries that trade without tariffs among themselves and apply a common tariff to outsiders, with free movement of goods, workers and capital.
The EEC system of guaranteed farm prices, intervention buying and support payments that shaped Irish farm incomes after 1973.
The EEC policy on access to fishing waters, total allowable catches and national quotas, agreed in full in January 1983.
The state fisheries board, set up in 1952 to develop the Irish fishing industry through grants, loans and training.
The maximum amount of a fish species that may be landed in a year in an area, fixed by the EEC and divided among states as quotas.
The principle that each member state keeps a fixed share of the total allowable catch of each species, based on past catches.
A limit on the amount of something, such as milk or fish, that a country or producer may produce or land.
The EEC fund created in 1975 to help poorer regions with infrastructure and industry.
The EEC directive of 1975 requiring equal pay for men and women for the same work or work of equal value.
A special exception from a general rule, such as Ireland's reserved fishing zone in the accession treaty.
